Each candidate is scored by running it in giri, a Go SSA interpreter, on 50 test vectors. It must return the reference result on every vector, and leave xs unchanged. Among correct candidates, a lower abstract cost (the number of SSA instructions executed over all vectors) scores higher, and any correct candidate scores above any incorrect one. The only import allowed is math/bits. Keep the function's name and signature.
responses:
## Analysis

The current program is a 16/8/4/2/1 unrolled popcount. The bounds-check hints in attempt 1 left the cost unchanged, which suggests the SSA prove pass already removes most bounds checks. The remaining per-block overhead is mainly the repeated reslicing `xs = xs[k:]`, which costs several SSA instructions (pointer offset, length, and capacity updates) each time it runs.

The proposed change keeps the same 16-wide unrolled body and the same tail structure, but uses a single integer index `i` for the main loop. Each 16-word block then costs one slice expression `xs[i : i+16]` instead of one reslice per block. Inside the block, the constant indices into `b` (length 16, known to the compiler) should not need per-element bounds checks. After the main loop, `xs = xs[i:]` hands the remainder to the same tail logic as before.

This is a targeted change to the main loop only. The correctness argument is unchanged: every word is counted exactly once, the tail still handles 0 to 15 remaining words, and `xs` is never written, so it is left unchanged.

I have not run giri, so the cost reduction is an estimate. If the SSA pass does not eliminate the bounds checks on `b`, the change may be neutral or slightly worse, and the replacement should be reverted.
